passage: For eight months Kiran told anyone who'd listen about the plan to transform education across the state. There was a forty-slide deck, three logo options, and a name argued over with Manoj, a friend, on long tea breaks. Kiran also had a full-time job and only Sunday mornings free. Whenever Manoj asked, 'What can we do this month?' Kiran said the idea was too big for small steps. Teaching one class felt silly next to a whole state. One Sunday a heavy monsoon kept the two indoors, and Manoj asked to see the calendar: not one meeting with a school, not one test of an idea. The deck was polished, and nothing else existed. Kiran closed the laptop and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How many logo options did Kiran have?
Why did Kiran resist small steps?
qa.a: Kiran felt the dream was so large that teaching one class seemed silly next to a whole state, so any first step felt too small.

qa.q: What other approach could Kiran use to get started?
qa.a: Kiran could pick one school and run a small pilot on a Sunday morning, since a real class would teach more than another version of the deck.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the deck and the months of talk?
qa.a: Manoj probably sees a lot of effort with nothing tested and feels frustrated, and asking to see the calendar shows worry for Kiran.

grounding: Shows a person with a huge dream to change education, months of presentations and logos, and no first action, because the size makes small steps seem pointless.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: grand vision with no first step [Pitfall]
passage:
In his rented room in Andheri, Eshaan had forty slides titled 'Transforming Education Across Maharashtra'. Three logo versions. A mission statement he rewrote every week. A plan for 10,000 schools in five years.
It was October. He had started in March.
His friend Rehana, a schoolteacher, came over and scrolled through the deck. 'It's beautiful,' she said. 'How many students have you taught?'
'None yet. I need funding first. And a team. And the app.'
'My school has a free slot on Saturdays. Twelve kids who need help with maths. You could start next week.'
Eshaan looked at the forty slides. Twelve kids felt almost embarrassing next to 10,000 schools. 'That's too small to matter,' he said.
Rehana closed the laptop. 'Eshaan, you've spent seven months on slides. Twelve is more than zero.'

qa.q: How many schools did Eshaan's plan cover?
Why did twelve kids feel 'almost embarrassing' to Eshaan?
qa.a: Next to his grand plan, a small start made Eshaan feel small and a little ashamed, as if it didn't count.

qa.q: What would you advise Eshaan to do next Saturday?
qa.a: Accept Rehana's offer and teach the twelve kids, learning what works before building anything bigger.

qa.q: How might Rehana see the forty slides?
qa.a: Rehana admires them but is frustrated that seven months of planning have helped no student yet.

grounding: It shows someone dreaming of transforming education across the state, spending months on slides and logos and never starting because first steps seem too small.

passage:
'Kavitha, how long have you been working on this "Water for Every Village" thing?'
'Eight months, Chandrika. The website's almost done. And the brand book.'
'Brand book?'
'Colours, fonts. We need to look serious when we go to big donors.'
'How many villages have water because of it?'
'...It's not launched yet. It's a national plan, it can't start small.'
'Why not?'
'Because one village doesn't change anything.'
'It changes things for that village. Paati's village has had a broken handpump since March. The panchayat just needs someone to follow up, and one mechanic.'
Kavitha looked at her laptop, at the logo glowing on the screen. 'That's not what the vision is.'
'Then the vision will stay on the screen,' Chandrika said gently.

qa.q: Since when has the handpump in Paati's village been broken?
How might Kavitha feel looking at the logo on the screen?
qa.a: Kavitha seems torn and defensive, attached to the big vision and uneasy that nothing has actually started.

qa.q: What small first step could Kavitha take?
qa.a: Kavitha could help Paati's village get the handpump fixed by following up with the panchayat and finding one mechanic.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika sees eight months of branding with no real help given, and gently worries the vision will never leave the screen.

grounding: It shows someone with a grand vision spending months on branding and never starting, because a first step seems too small.
